extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and practitioners who represent clients before the USPTO in trademark (and related patent) matters, particularly U.S. counsel for foreign-domiciled trademark applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements governing practitioner competence, signature compliance, supervision, candor, client communication, and sanctions for trademark practice before the USPTO; includes specific USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct provisions and imposed probation conditions. Useful for assessing practitioner compliance and disciplinary risk in USPTO trademark matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (requirement of U.S.-licensed attorney for foreign-domiciled trademark applicants/registrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-domiciled trademark applicants or registrants must be represented before the USPTO by an attorney who is licensed to practice law in the United States. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a); Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 Fed. Reg. 31498 (July 2, 2019) ("the U.S. Counsel Rule").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy objectives include instilling public confidence that U.S. registrations issued to foreign applicants are not subject to invalidation (e.g., improper signatures) and ensuring foreign applicants are assisted only by authorized practitioners subject to USPTO disciplinary rules. The USPTO has published guidance and rulemaking; practitioners representing foreign-domiciled clients are expected to know and follow these requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO trademark signature rules (personal entry requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory and a person electronically signing via TEAS must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission. See 37 C.F.R. § 2.193(a) and (c), and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP §611.01(c) gives unequivocal direction that the person(s) identified as the signatory must personally enter the signatory's electronic signature, either directly on the TEAS form or in the emailed form. A person may not delegate signature authority, no person may sign or enter the name of another, typing another's electronic signature is not a valid signature, and use of document-signing software by another person to generate the named signatory's electronic signature is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: TMEP direction against third-party signing (explicit proscription)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure (TMEP) expressly proscribes any person other than the named signatory from signing trademark documents filed with the USPTO and states that another person may not use document-signing software to create or generate the electronic signature of the named signatory. See TMEP §611.01(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP is a primary reference for trademark practitioners; the guidance is repeatedly updated and was available to Respondent. Practitioners should consult the TMEP for signature requirements and examples of improper practices and sanctions cited in Board/USPTO decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations in trademark applications are signed under penalty of perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications contain declarations signed under penalty of perjury; false statements are subject to punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001, and signatories make specific representations regarding use or intent to use a mark in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO relies on such declarations when examining applications and issuing registrations; therefore practitioners must ensure accuracy and proper execution of declarations because misstatements affect registrability and may carry criminal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.303)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner's ethical obligation of candor includes that it is misconduct to knowingly make a false statement of fact to a tribunal (e.g., the USPTO) or fail to correct a false statement of material fact previously made, and in an ex parte proceeding a practitioner shall inform the tribunal of all material facts known that will enable the tribunal to make an informed decision, whether or not the facts are adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED correspondence cited §11.303 when notifying Respondent; practitioners must correct or disclose material facts and cannot withhold facts adverse to a matter before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate with clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's ethical obligations regarding communicating with clients include the duty to keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter and the duty to explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent received OED correspondence about signature issues and delayed communicating with clients; practitioners are expected to timely inform clients when issues affecting filings or rights arise and explain implications so clients can decide on representation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must provide competent representation to a client. Failure to understand adequately the USPTO trademark signature rules or TMEP direction, and presenting trademark documents that violate those rules, violates §11.101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent representation includes being familiar with applicable procedural and signature rules relevant to trademark prosecution and the TMEP; lack of knowledge of widely published USPTO requirements is actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence requirement (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client. Presenting trademark documents (including declarations) that violate USPTO trademark signature rules and TMEP direction can constitute a failure of reasonable diligence under §11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diligence includes adequate processes and verification before submitting filings and timely responses to identified issues raised by the Office or third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities over non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who is a partner or has supervisory authority must make reasonable efforts to ensure the firm has measures giving reasonable assurance that non-practitioner's conduct is compatible with the practitioner's professional obligations and must adequately supervise non-practitioner assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes implementing adequate controls and measures to prevent paralegals or staff from entering a practitioner's signature on trademark documents and sworn declarations presented to the USPTO. Failure to supervise adequately is a rule violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation. Presenting trademark documents that were signed by other than the named signatory constitutes misrepresentation under §11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP and USPTO guidance state that typing another's electronic signature or permitting another to sign in the practitioner's name is not the named signatory's signature; such conduct is treated as a misrepresentation to the USPTO even if done without wrongful intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to USPTO trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration system. Presenting improperly signed trademark documents (including declarations) may be prejudicial under §11.804(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO views substantive signature compliance as integral to the integrity of the registration process; violations can harm applicants' and registrants' IP rights and the system's integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature rule is substantive (not technical) and noncompliance can be misrepresentation even without wrongful intent
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO trademark signature rule requiring the named signatory to enter his or her signature on a trademark document is a substantive rule, not a technical requirement; a failure to enter the named signatory's signature—even without wrongful intent—is a misrepresentation under 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) and potentially adversely affects trademark rights and the integrity of the USPTO process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners cannot treat signature requirements as mere formality; inadvertent or well-intentioned delegations that result in another entering the signature are still disciplinary risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner's duty to be aware of widely published USPTO resources and expected knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners who represent applicants, registrants, or others before the USPTO in trademark matters are reasonably expected to know (a) the applicable trademark prosecution rules; (b) the provisions of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct implicated by representation; and (c) the potential disciplinary consequences when such provisions are violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO publishes ample information (webpages, TMEP, rulemaking, OED FOIA documents); practitioners are expected to use these resources and maintain updated knowledge of applicable rules and guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for violations: public reprimand and probation (and suspension procedures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary outcomes may include public reprimand and probation; the OED can issue an Order to Show Cause and request immediate suspension for up to twelve months if the practitioner fails to comply with probation conditions, the Final Order, or USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This Final Order imposed a public reprimand and twenty (20) months' probation; probationary violations can trigger an administrative show-cause process and possible suspension. Past USPTO orders demonstrate consistent discipline for similar signature and supervision violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — bi-weekly USPTO trademark search and prompt reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: During the first twelve (12) months of probation, the respondent shall, at least on a bi-weekly basis, (i) search the USPTO's online trademark search system for applications identifying him as the attorney of record; and (ii) promptly inform in writing the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy of each trademark document filing identifying him as the attorney of record that was filed without his knowledge or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a monitoring/mitigation measure intended to detect filings made in the practitioner's name without authorization and to notify the Office so corrective steps can be taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — bi-monthly written reports to OED about searches
rubrics_metrics.description: While on probation, the respondent shall, at least on a bi-monthly basis, submit a written report to the OED Director stating completion of the bi-weekly searches and, as applicable: (i) that no improper filings were identified; or (ii) providing copies of correspondence sent to the USPTO Office of Trademark Examination Policy regarding any improper filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These reports serve as proof of compliance with the monitoring requirement and create a traceable record of remediation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — client notification attestations and documentary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent must, within specified timeframes, submit written declarations (per 28 U.S.C. § 1746) attesting to the extent to which YaYi forwarded information about the improperly signed documents to Respondent's foreign-domiciled trademark clients, and provide documentary proof (copies of the written correspondence transmitted to each client). If attestations are not provided within 60 days, Respondent must forward the information to affected clients in their native language within 90 days and provide attestations/proof within 120 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition requires affirmative notice to affected clients and documentary evidence of such notice, using mailing/email addresses from the "Applicant's Information" portion of the trademark application (not third-party addresses), and translations where appropriate. Email may be used only if the address reasonably belongs to and is directly accessible by the client (not a referring entity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — review of TMEP and declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Within 30 days of the Final Order, Respondent shall provide to the OED Director a written declaration (per 28 U.S.C. § 1746) stating that he has reviewed thoroughly all provisions of the Trademark Manual of Examining Procedure, including provisions pertaining to the USPTO's signature requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a documented attestation that the practitioner has familiarized himself with TMEP guidance relevant to the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — continuing legal education (CLE) on ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Within ninety (90) days of the Final Order, Respondent shall provide a written declaration that he has successfully completed two (2) hours of continuing legal education credit on ethics/professional responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short CLE on ethics/professional responsibility is required to remediate knowledge gaps implicated by the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — completion of USPTO Trademark Basics Boot Camp
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to termination of probation, Respondent shall provide a written declaration that he has enrolled in, virtually attended, and completed each of the eight modules comprising the USPTO's Trademark Basics Boot Camp (available on the USPTO website).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completion of USPTO-offered training modules is required as part of remediation and ongoing competence in trademark prosecution practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probation condition — cooperation with USPTO inquiries regarding third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with the USPTO in any present or future inquiry into YaYi or any other third-party entities or persons with whom Respondent worked or was solicited to work in connection with patent or trademark documents submitted to the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full cooperation includes providing information, documents, and assistance requested by OED or other USPTO offices investigating related misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for public notice/publication of disciplinary orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order at the OED's electronic FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the proposed notice describing the reprimand, probation, and factual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is part of USPTO's transparency and serves to notify practitioners and public of the disciplinary outcome and the conduct that led to it.
